title: Biological Methodologies
purpose: Seed biological research methods across molecular, cellular, organismal, population, ecological and evolutionary scales so Lantern can select evidence appropriate to living systems while preserving historical contingency, variation and scale.

concepts.definition: Level of organization such as molecule, cell, tissue, organism, population, community, ecosystem or lineage; inference may not transfer automatically across scales.
Manipulative study of biological systems under controlled or semi-controlled conditions.
Observation/measurement/experimentation in natural environments where ecological context is retained but control may be reduced.
Systematic comparison across organisms, populations or lineages to investigate patterns, mechanisms and evolutionary history.
A species/system studied intensively because it is experimentally tractable or informative; findings require justification before generalization to other organisms.
Evidence from DNA/RNA/proteins/metabolites and molecular interactions under validated assays.
Evidence concerning cell structures, states, processes and interactions.
Observed/measured characteristics produced through interactions among genotype, development and environment.
Genetic constitution at specified loci/genomic scope; genotype does not uniquely determine most complex phenotypes.
A scoped group of organisms/genes considered for demographic, ecological or evolutionary analysis.
Biological variation among members of a population; population summaries do not define every individual.
Differential reproductive contribution associated with heritable variation under environmental conditions, producing population-level evolutionary change.
Stochastic change in allele frequencies, especially influential in finite populations.
Movement of genetic variation among populations through migration/reproduction.
A heritable trait/process shaped by selection because it contributed to reproductive success in relevant ancestral/current contexts; not every useful trait is necessarily an adaptation.
Context-dependent reproductive contribution relative to alternatives; not moral worth, strength or universal superiority.
Similarity due to shared evolutionary ancestry.
Functional/structural similarity evolved independently rather than inherited from the same ancestral feature.
Inference of evolutionary relationships/history using characters, sequences and explicit models.
Interaction among organisms and environments including competition, predation, mutualism, parasitism and facilitation.
Explanation of how biological components/processes produce an outcome.
Explanation concerning historical origins, selection, drift, constraint or lineage processes.
Explanation of how traits/processes arise across an organism's development.

guards.reason: Population summaries describe distributions, not every member.
Complex phenotypes commonly depend on development, environment, interactions and probabilistic processes.
Current usefulness alone does not establish historical origin by natural selection.
Evolution has no general requirement of foresight or predetermined progress.
Biological fitness is context-dependent reproductive success, not universal superiority.
Drift, gene flow, mutation, recombination and other processes can contribute.
Similarity can arise through convergence/analogy; ancestry evidence is required.
Generalization depends on conserved mechanisms, lineage differences and scope.
Environmental complexity and interactions can change biological effects.
Proximate mechanism and evolutionary history answer different questions.
Association can reflect linkage, population structure, interactions and complex causation.
Species concepts differ in applicability across sexual, asexual, fossil and hybridizing lineages.

invariants: Population distributions do not define every individual.
Genotype, phenotype, development and environment remain distinct interacting concepts.
Evolutionary change is population/lineage change across generations, not goal-directed improvement.
Natural selection is one evolutionary mechanism among several.
Biological fitness is environment/scope dependent and not normative worth.
Current usefulness does not by itself establish adaptation.
Similarity does not establish homology without ancestry evidence.
Model-organism findings require justified transport to other organisms.
Mechanistic, developmental and evolutionary explanations answer different but compatible questions.
Field and laboratory evidence have different strengths and scopes.
Phylogenetic relatedness can violate naive independence assumptions in cross-species comparisons.

provenance.authoring_basis: Core experimental, field, comparative, evolutionary, population, molecular and ecological biological methodologies adapted to Lantern's multi-scale scientific architecture.
